why_this_file_declares_no_leg_yet:
SUPERSEDED BY `leg` AND `the_sub_populations_this_file_records`, WHICH C1c-iv-a DECLARED. Kept as the record of what was true for the four slices that could not declare them, because the reasoning is what makes the present assertion mean something.

WHAT IT SAID, and it was accurate at each of its tips: `leg` and the sub-population block are both-or-neither, and declaring `leg: server` turns G22b on — the generator then evaluates `all_of[{leg equals server}]` fresh against B2b and refuses the build unless EVERY server ET-CC member has a row here. While the file held 59, then 64, then 80, then 111 of the leg's 145, declaring the leg would have correctly REDDENED the build, so `leg_totality!` reported NOT ASSERTED — the honest state of a partial leg and not a gap. What that COST was stated rather than absorbed: G22b is the guard that catches a member silently missing from the LEG, and it could not fire on this file; G15a still bit, comparing the derived population against the file's own selector in both directions, and it is strictly weaker.

WHAT IS TRUE NOW: the file holds all 145, the block is declared, and G22b fires at every build. The cost named above is paid off, and that it is paid off is itself shown rather than asserted — `crosswalk_controls.exs totality` plants a server row in a TWENTY-SECOND module, measures G15a green at 145 against 145 and G22b red at 146 against 145 on that one input, and drives the generator to a non-zero OS exit on it.
what_C1c_i_establishes_for_C1c_ii_iii_an: This is the FIRST server-leg ticket and three things it settles are inherited rather than re-decided. (1) THE FILE: one edges file for the whole server leg, this one, appended to by each later slice — not one per ticket, which would split the leg by the accident of which member was adjudicated first. (2) THE MEMBER SELECTOR: `all_of[{leg equals server}, any_of[{key starts_with "<Module>/"} ...]]`, evaluated against B2b. The server rows carry no `cg` and no `tokens` — measured, all 145 — and `leg_reason` partitions by code path rather than by OC scenario, so no `equals` predicate over the anchor denotes a server sub-population at all; the module does, and modules partition the leg exactly (21 of them, keys unique, no prefix collision with the trailing `/`). A later slice adds its modules to the `any_of` and changes nothing else. (3) THE AXIS-EXTRACTION METHOD, which is written out in `oc-axes-c1.json`'s own `scope.how_the_18_were_cut` rather than here, because that is where its inputs live. C1c-ii INHERITED all three without amendment and the fact is recorded here rather than argued again: it appended to this file rather than opening a second, it added ONE module clause to the `any_of` and changed nothing else about the member selector's shape, and it cut its 36 axis rows by the method `oc-axes-c1.json`'s `how_the_18_were_cut` states. The one thing it did NOT inherit is the check selector's single clause: the MRTR family is fourteen scenarios, so the `any_of` went from one clause to fifteen, and `why_fourteen_clauses_and_not_a_prefix` says why that is enumeration and not a prefix test. C1c-iii inherited all three the same way — it appended to this file, it added FOUR module clauses to the `any_of` and changed nothing else about the member selector's shape, and it cut its 41 axis rows by the same method. It extended the check selector from fifteen clauses to thirty-four on the same enumerate-never-prefix ground, and measured what the prefix form would have cost today rather than only in future: a `starts_with` over `tools-` admits `tools-call-with-logging`, `tools-call-sampling` and `tools-call-elicitation`, three scenarios in this very build that are NOT in its 41.
why_the_leg_conjunct_is_load_bearing:

THE CHANGE OF KIND IS THE POINT, AND IT IS WHY THIS FIELD IS RE-MEASURED RATHER THAN CARRIED. Through C1c-iii-b the same measurement was 113 rows and TWO strays, and both strays were single rows in modules that are otherwise wholly server — so the conjunct was kept on REASONING, with almost nothing live behind it. the_population_this_file_declares.how_the_leg_closes: IT HAS CLOSED. The twenty-one modules declared here hold all 145 of the leg's members and there is no twenty-second: G22b evaluates `leg equals server` fresh against B2b at every build and refuses if the two sets differ in either direction. The MODULE cut is a PARTITION — 59 + 5 + 16 + 31 + 34 = 145 over the five C1c slices, no module in two of them, because a module prefix denotes disjoint key sets. the_population_this_file_declares.why_the_cut_is_by_MODULE_and_not_by_SCEN: The dispatch asked for `leg=server AND the server-stateless scenario` and that predicate is NOT EXECUTABLE over the anchor: B2b's rows carry cg, cg_basis, contradicts_oc, key, leg, leg_reason and tokens — no scenario field — and `selected!/4` hard-refuses a member selector whose source is not the attribution file. `cg` is null on all 145 server rows and `tokens` is empty on all 145, so neither discriminates; `leg_reason` has ten values and partitions by CODE PATH (59 and 39 on the two dispatch/plug ones), which is not the same cut as the OC scenario. The MODULE is already in the anchor — `key` is `Module/test` — so a prefix predicate over `key` denotes the slice, and PM-ratified on 2026-09-23 it is the pattern the rest of the leg follows. the_population_this_file_declares.what_the_trailing_slash_buys_and_what_it: Each prefix ends in `/`, and the reason is PROSPECTIVE rather than live — stated that way because the first draft of this field claimed otherwise and the control measured it out. The claim was that without the slash `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTP` would name both MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest and MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTP.ACTest. That string is not one of the prefixes this selector uses: the leaves carry FULL module names, and over all 21 server modules — over all 30 in B2b — NOT ONE is a plain string-prefix of another. RE-MEASURED at C1c-iv-a with all TWENTY-ONE leaves in place, over all 30 modules in B2b, and the answer is unchanged: NOT ONE declared module name is a plain string-prefix of another, and not one of B2b's 30 is a prefix of another either. That is the point of re-measuring rather than carrying it — this slice added the seven likeliest counter-examples in the register, `MCP.ProtocolTest` among them, and `MCP.ProtocolTest` is NOT a prefix of `MCP.Protocol.MetaTest` because the character after the shared `MCP.Protocol` differs (`T` against `.`). It was close enough to be worth measuring rather than assuming. `mix run conformance/controls/crosswalk_controls.exs selectors` strips the slash from every leaf and measures the population unchanged, so on the shipped anchor the slash removes NOTHING. What it buys is a bound against a module ADDED LATER whose name EXTENDS one of these twenty-one — `...DispatchTestExtra` and the like. That case has no live instance, so the control CONSTRUCTS one: a synthetic server row in an extending module, refused by the slashed selector and admitted by the slashless one, on the same fixture and in both directions. The slash is therefore kept as a discipline whose value is future, and NOT as a fact about this anchor.
the_population_this_file_declares.why_a_prefix_predicate_and_not_an_enumer: An enumeration of `key equals` leaves needs no new code and was rejected for the reason C1b-iii's `cg is_null` was chosen over one: an enumeration CANNOT DENOTE A MEMBER ADDED LATER. A new test in one of these twenty-one modules would fall silently outside the population, and G15a — which compares the derived population against the selector's denotation — would stay green over the omission, because the omission would be in the universe as well as in the file. The prefix predicate picks the new member up and G15a then reds naming it as `missing`. The cost is one new selector leaf, and the leaf's caller is the population it was added for, so it is not S9-15's guard on a dead path. AND THE TWO HALVES ARE NOW BOTH SHOWN, which they were not while the leg was open: a new test in an EXISTING declared module is caught by G15a, a new MODULE only by G22b, and `crosswalk_controls.exs totality` drives the second case — a planted B2b row in a TWENTY-SECOND module, G15a green at 145 against 145 and G22b red at 146 against 145 on that one input. Neither guard alone reaches both shapes, which is the standing argument for keeping the prefix predicate rather than collapsing the selector to `leg equals server`.

selector.the_bound_this_leaves: THERE IS NO LONGER A SCENARIO BOUND, and that is a change of kind rather than of size. Until this slice the declared CHECK population was a PROPER subset of the server leg, so a bucket-1 row meant `no counterpart among these N` and not `no counterpart on our leg`, and FOUR rows were scoped that way and said so in their `kind`: SRV02 and SRV18 named REAL counterparts in `dns-rebinding-protection`, SRV07 and SRV20 in `caching`, each so that whichever later C1c slice declared those scenarios would inherit the member rather than re-search for it. selector.why_fourteen_clauses_and_not_a_prefix: A prefix clause would be SHORTER and would declare a DIFFERENT population: every future scenario whose name begins `input-required-result-` would join this file's declared checks the moment a harness bump introduced it, and would then have to be axis-decomposed by G19 or redden a build nobody had changed. Enumerating costs fourteen lines and makes the population a decision this ticket took rather than a pattern that keeps deciding. The same reasoning is why the client file enumerates its seven.
selector.why_the_feature_endpoint_scenarios_are_e: NINETEEN more equality clauses and not three `starts_with` ones. A prefix over `tools-` would be three lines instead of eight and would declare a DIFFERENT population: every future scenario a harness bump named `tools-call-something` would join this file's declared checks the moment it appeared, and would then have to be axis-decomposed by G19 or redden a build nobody had changed. The cost is real and is paid knowingly — the prefix would also have silently ADMITTED `tools-call-with-logging`, `tools-call-sampling` and `tools-call-elicitation`, three scenarios that exist in this very build and are NOT in this slice's 41. That is not a hypothetical about a future bump; it is a live mis-declaration the prefix form would have made today.
selector.why_the_three_misc_scenarios_are_enumera: THREE more equality clauses and not a `starts_with` or a bare `leg equals server`. The bare-leg form is the tempting one now that the denotation IS the leg, and it is refused for the reason `why_the_selector_is_still_a_union_of_slices` gives on the member side: the enumeration and the leg are two different questions that happen to have the same answer today, and collapsing them would make the check population a pattern that keeps deciding rather than a decision this file's tickets took. It also has a live cost. A harness bump adding a thirty-eighth server scenario would join this population silently under the bare-leg form and would then have to be axis-decomposed by G19 or redden a build nobody had changed; under the enumeration it falls outside, and the file says so. The same reasoning that rejected a `tools-` prefix at C1c-iii, applied to the case where the prefix would be the empty string.

what_a_record_carries_and_why.claim: ONE claim within the member (A3 §1). A member making several contributes several edges and they are never collapsed.
what_a_record_carries_and_why.tag: the OC check's token, re-derived and required to equal the stored one.
what_a_record_carries_and_why.axes: one verdict per axis of the check's decomposition — `agrees`, `contradicts` or `silent`. The set must be the decomposition's WHOLE set.
what_a_record_carries_and_why.et_verdict: green on every record here: all 145 members are green at the accepted run — RE-MEASURED at C1c-iv-a over the CLOSED leg rather than carried from C1c-iii-b's 111 or C1c-iii's 80 — which is why buckets 3 and 6 are empty by construction. The measurement is `mix test` over the leg's 21 modules, run at the delivered tip; the seven this slice adds are 0 failures each, as are the two holding the four members it moved out of bucket 1.
what_a_record_carries_and_why.evidence: the ET assertion, cited by line span, and the OC conjunct it meets. Every quoted byte-string is verbatim at an address the evidence itself names (G30).
what_a_record_carries_and_why.not_carried: `oc_key`, `shape`, `bucket` — all three are derived by the generator and refused if stored.
what_a_record_carries_and_why.note: used where a record needs something said about it that is not its evidence — an escalation, a measured surprise, a bound.
what_a_record_carries_and_why.why_contradicts_and_not_silent: carried by the three contradicting edges, because that is the judgement a reader is most likely to want to disagree with.
what_a_record_carries_and_why.authored_by: the ticket. Present on every record MES-105 authored and ABSENT on the four C1a inherited from crosswalk-edges.json, which is how the client file marks its own inherited rows — provenance readable by the field's absence rather than by a second copy of the ticket key.

how_a_silent_axis_was_decided: The client file's rule, applied unchanged and NOT restated here: a claim covers an axis only when an assertion's SUBJECT is the behaviour that axis names. What IS new on this leg is how often the rule bites on one axis of a two-axis check, and it bites the same way every time: eight of this file's red-OC edges are silent on an `http_status` axis and agree on a `jsonrpc_error_code` one. That is not a coincidence, it is the shape of this SDK's suite — `MCP.Server.DispatchTest` asserts below the transport and cannot see a status, and `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest` reads `error(conn)` rather than `conn.status` on every removed-method path. It is a real gap in our coverage and it is what puts those edges in 4b rather than leaving them able to reach 4a. C1c-ii's 16 edges bite a different way and it is worth recording because it changes what a `silent` MEANS on this file. Its two members make eight claims between them against multi-axis checks, and 29 of its 63 axis verdicts are `silent` — but almost none of those silences is a coverage gap. They are the arithmetic of A3 §1: a claim is ONE assertion, a check has up to five axes, and a member whose three claims cover three different axes of one check contributes three edges each silent on the other axes. Read edge by edge that looks like thin coverage; read member by member, `InputRequiredResultRequestStateIncomplete` has ALL FIVE of its axes covered by some claim of the stateless member. The file does not collapse them, because collapsing is what A3 §1 forbids — but a reader counting silences should count them per MEMBER, not per edge.
the_all_silent_case:
FOUR edges have EVERY axis silent, over THREE distinct checks — `ServerUnsupportedVersionError` carries two of them. They are recorded and ESCALATED as `no_axis_contact`, never bucketed — A3 §2 rules that covering zero of one axis is no match rather than a partial one, generalised to N axes is exactly this, and A3 §3's table has no row for it. What differs from the client leg is that TWO of the four here are against a check that is RED at the accepted run (`ServerUnsupportedVersionError`), so the silence is not harmless: it is the precise reason our green tells us nothing about why the harness failed us. Each of the four says on its own record what the near-agreement was and where it stopped.

THE FOURTH IS THIS SLICE'S OWN AND IT IS THE +1 IN ESCALATED 14 → 15: `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest`'s AC7 ordering claim against `DNSRebindingRejected`, whose single axis is silent because the axis scores the HTTP status on the wire and the claim scores WHEN in the pipeline that status was decided. It is against a check that is GREEN at the accepted run — and so is `MCP.Server.CapabilityHonestyTest`'s `DiscoverCapabilitiesMatchHandlers`, so TWO of the four are against a GREEN check and TWO against a RED one, and that closes over four. What is unique to THIS one is its authorship and not its colour: it is the only one of the four THIS SLICE authored, the other three being C1c-i's. This field read THREE at MES-117's delivered tip: the slice authored the row that falsified it, REPORTED that row as the escalation +1, and did not re-count the field — caught in review, re-measured here, and the cause named in `why_the_figure_sweep_missed_four_fields`.

THE CLIENT FIGURE IS RE-MEASURED HERE TOO AND IT IS NOT WHAT THIS FIELD USED TO SAY. The field read "The client file has four of these"; measured at this tip `conformance/data/crosswalk-edges-client.json` carries SEVEN all-silent edges over FOUR distinct checks, so the four was the CHECK count and the sentence spent it as an EDGE count. The rule applied there is the same one. RECORDED AND NOT FIXED BEYOND THIS FILE: the client file's own `the_all_silent_case` still reads "Four edges have EVERY axis silent" at this tip, which is the identical ambiguity one file further out, and that file belongs to the client-leg tickets — MES-117 corrects its own prose and moves no figure outside its own leg.
the_contradicting_edges:
SIX edges carry a `contradicts` verdict. FIVE are C1c-i's and are unchanged: the `initialize` pair (inherited from C1a) answering -32022 where the suite requires -32601; the `RequestMetaInvalid` pair answering -32022 where -32602 is required; and `subscriptions/listen` in JSON mode asserting HTTP 200 where the check's `http_status` axis requires 404 while AGREEING with the same check's `jsonrpc_error_code` axis. All five are 4a — red OC, green ET — and none escalates, because `(red, green, :contradicting)` is a row the ratified table has.

THE SIXTH IS C1c-ii's AND IT IS A DIFFERENT ANIMAL: it is the crosswalk's first contradiction against a GREEN check, and the first against `WireSchemaValid` on either leg. `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest/test tools/call input-required → retry with requestState → completion` asserts `is_list(first["inputRequests"])`, and the pinned schema's `InputRequests` is `type: object`. So our unit asserts, and passes on, a message that the check's own predicate would count as a violation — while the check is SUCCESS at the accepted run, because the harness ran against `conformance/server_handler.ex`, which sends a map and says in its own moduledoc that the SDK's `@spec` disagrees with the wire type. A contradiction against a GREEN check is NOT A BUCKET AT ALL, and that was measured rather than predicted: `MatchKey.bucket/3` sends `(:green, :green, :contradicting)` to `{:escalate, :inconsistent_verdict_pair}` (match_key.ex:554), so the edge leaves the bucket arithmetic entirely and lands in `escalations`. That is the right home for it — BOTH SIDES PASSED and they disagree, which is an inconsistency in the evidence rather than a verdict about the implementation — and it is the SERVER leg's first instance of that escalation (the client leg has three, all against `ClientMcpNameHeader_tools_call`). It is also why this finding is invisible to anyone reading bucket counts alone, and why it is written out here.
why_contradicts_and_not_silent: `how_a_silent_axis_was_decided` is conservative about claiming COVERAGE — a claim covers an axis only when an assertion's SUBJECT is the behaviour that axis names. It is NOT a rule for suppressing disagreement, and reading it that way would make it a rule for hiding exactly what a crosswalk exists to find. The client file states this and it is cited rather than restated; what is new here is that it now decides FIVE edges instead of three, and that on this leg the two readings give visibly different answers. Each of the five carries its own `why_contradicts_and_not_silent` where the judgement is not obvious from the evidence. C1c-ii's single contradiction is where the two readings come apart most sharply, and the edge carries its own `why_contradicts_and_not_silent` for it. The conservative reading would say the unit is `silent` on schema validity because it asserts a VALUE and not a VALIDATION. That reading is available and it is wrong: the axis quantifies over every message the implementation sent, the unit asserts the content of one such message, and the content it asserts is one the axis's predicate rejects. There is no grain at which the two are about different things — and the whole point of `how_a_silent_axis_was_decided` being about COVERAGE is that it must not become a way of not noticing this.
what_the_red_OC_population_did_and_did_n:
This is the first slice with a substantial red-OC population — 17 FAILURE and 13 SUCCESS among the declared checks, against 54 of 54 SUCCESS across the whole client leg — so it is the first at which buckets 4a and 4b are reachable on real data. Both are: 5 edges land 4a and 6 land 4b, out of 13 edges against a red check. A3 §3's THIRD combination, `(red, green, :full) -> :divergent_despite_agreement`, is STILL NOT LIVE, and that is a MEASUREMENT rather than an oversight. For it to fire, an edge would have to agree with EVERY axis of a red check. Every red check reached here either has a single axis our claims contradict (the RequestMetaInvalid family — we answer -32022 where -32602 is required) or has an `http_status` axis no unit of ours asserts: 8 of the 13 red-OC edges are silent on exactly that axis. The one unit that DOES assert a status asserts the wrong one, which is a contradiction and not an agreement. So the combination is unreachable from this slice's claims, and saying so is worth more than manufacturing an edge to reach it. The escalation is nonetheless EXERCISED on real server-stateless data by `conformance/controls/crosswalk_falsification_controls.exs escalations`, which takes a real 4b edge from this file, mutates its silent `http_status` axis to `agrees` in memory and requires the escalation to fire, then mutates the OC verdict to green on the same edge and requires it to STOP firing and bucket as 5. Both directions, because a rule that fires on everything is not discriminating and a control that only shows it firing cannot tell the difference.

C1c-ii ADDS NO RED-OC EDGE AT ALL, and the reason is a measurement rather than a choice. Of the 36 checks it declares, TWO are red at the accepted run and both are in one scenario: `InputRequiredResultNonToolIncomplete` (FAILURE) and that scenario's own `WireSchemaValid` (FAILURE). Both are about `prompts/get` returning an InputRequiredResult, and BOTH of this slice's members drive `tools/call` only — our SDK's `prompts/get` handler has no `{:input_required, …}` clause, which `conformance/server_handler.ex` records as a known limitation. So the family's red population is not merely unreached: there is no unit of ours that could reach it. A3 §3's `(red, green, :full)` — `divergent_despite_agreement` — is therefore STILL not live, and for a THIRD distinct reason: C1c-i's red checks were reached and contradicted, C1c-i's others had an `http_status` axis nobody asserts, and here the red checks are never exercised. Reporting the measured zero is worth more than manufacturing an edge to reach it, and the escalation machinery is exercised on real data by `crosswalk_falsification_controls.exs escalations` regardless.

BUT THE DISTANCE TO IT HAS CHANGED, and that is worth recording because C1c-i called it unreachable. FIVE of this slice's edges are shape `:full` — they agree with every axis of their check — and all five sit on GREEN checks, so `(red, green, :full)` is ONE OC VERDICT away rather than out of reach: MEASURED by `crosswalk_falsification_controls.exs warning_mapping`, patching `IgnoreUnexpectedParams` from WARNING to FAILURE makes its `:full` edge escalate as `divergent_despite_agreement` on the spot. That is a mutation and not a finding — the committed data still has no live instance — but `unreachable from this slice's claims` would now be the wrong description of why.

C1c-iii ADDS NOTHING TO 4a OR 4b, AND THE MEASUREMENT BEHIND THAT IS LEG-WIDE RATHER THAN SLICE-LOCAL — see `the_red_oc_population_of_the_server_leg_is_now_closed`.

C1c-iii-b ADDS NOTHING TO 4a OR 4b EITHER, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS PER MEMBER RATHER THAN INHERITED. Its nine edges sit on three checks and all three are SUCCESS; its 31 members drive `MCP.Server.Dispatch` directly over `tools/list` and `tools/call` and reach no HTTP status, no `prompts/get` and no `_meta` validation, which is what the nineteen FAILUREs are about. The working is in `the_escalation_is_now_a_bound_and_C1c_iv_owns_the_last_chance`, which this slice also corrects from 65 to 34.

edges.claim: that InputRequiredResult carries `inputRequests`, and the SDK puts that value on the wire as a JSON ARRAY
edges.evidence: streamable_http_stateless_test.exs:248 — `assert is_list(first["inputRequests"])`, where `first` is the decoded body of a real HTTP response our `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTP.Plug` produced (streamable_http_stateless_test.exs:245 — `first = post(opts(), rpc("tools/call", with_meta(%{"name" => "needs_input"}))) |> result()`). The axis filters the validator's violation list by `origin`, keeping only violations attributed to the implementation: every message OUR side put on the wire must validate against the pinned spec schema. The binding definition is addressed on the axis row as `input_requests_schema_definition`, and it declares `InputRequests` an object type whose `additionalProperties` reference `InputRequest`. A JSON ARRAY is not an object, so the message this assertion is about is one the axis's predicate rejects, and the unit asserts it and PASSES.
edges.why_contradicts_and_not_silent: Same subject, and they disagree. The axis's subject is the schema validity of a message the implementation SENT; this assertion's subject is the content of a message the implementation sent. `how_a_silent_axis_was_decided` is conservative about claiming COVERAGE, not a rule for suppressing disagreement — and the conservative reading does not rescue this one, because there is no grain at which the two are about different things. Recording it `silent` would be the false statement.
edges.note:
THE FIRST ET CLAIM IN THE CROSSWALK TO CONTRADICT `WireSchemaValid`, and three things about it have to be said or it will be misread.
(1) WHY THE CHECK IS GREEN AT THE ACCEPTED RUN. The harness ran against `conformance/server_handler.ex`, which sends a MAP — the file says so itself: ``MRTR.input_required/2` is spec'd `list() | nil` while the wire type `InputRequests` is a JSON object keyed by input name. This file sends a map, per the schema.` So the conformance adapter and this unit disagree with EACH OTHER about the SDK's own wire shape, and the accepted run only ever saw the adapter.
(2) WHY IT IS THE SDK'S PROPERTY AND NOT THE FIXTURE'S. `MCP.Protocol.Messages.MRTR.input_required/2` is `@spec input_required(list() | nil, binary() | nil)` and puts the value through untouched. The list is what the SDK's own type says to pass; a handler that follows the spec is contradicting the spec of the function it calls.
(3) WHICH OF THE FOURTEEN `WireSchemaValid` ROWS. The contradiction holds against ALL FOURTEEN of the family's `WireSchemaValid` rows, because all fourteen are one generic validator and the offending message would be the same in every scenario. ONE edge is filed, against the `input-required-result-request-state` row, because that is the scenario whose flow this unit mirrors — a `requestState` round trip. Fourteen edges would be one finding counted fourteen times and would inflate every figure this file reports; recording the scope here is the alternative to both.

edges.evidence: content_test.exs:42 — `decoded["type"] == "text"` — and content_test.exs:43 — `decoded["text"] == "test"`. The struct is built at content_test.exs:38 with no type field given, so the discriminator is SYNTHESISED on encode rather than echoed from the input, which is what makes this a claim about the SDK rather than about the fixture. Those two assertions are the check's two content-block axes: the harness selects a block whose type is the wire literal `text` and then requires that block's text field to be non-empty. edges.evidence: json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:447 — `assert errored["isError"] == true` — where the result comes from json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:444 — `{errored, error_log} = with_log(fn -> call("raw_extras", %{"extras" => true}) end)`, a slot 3 that is the bare boolean rather than a map. An identity test against true, which is this check's isError axis. The second axis is about the error result's FIRST content block carrying a non-empty text field — the failure being DESCRIBED and not merely flagged — and this unit asserts nothing about content at all. Its result's content array is empty, but it is empty BY CONSTRUCTION: the tool is driven with an empty content list on the same line, so the handler returns exactly what the unit handed it. The axis quantifies over the content of a result from a tool that described its failure; this unit's subject is the isError flag's round trip. Silent by the GRAIN of the claim, not by a reading of it.
edges.note: THE OTHER DIRECTION OF THIS MEMBER REACHES NO AXIS, AND THAT IS THE COVERAGE RESULT. json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:449 pins that a FALSE boolean slot 3 leaves NO isError on the wire. `ToolsCallError` scores only the error case, and no check in the declared population asks what a successful result must NOT carry, so the false half is unmatched. It is the same absent-versus-false fact the extras-map member records at json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:238 and it is not given a second home here.

edges.claim: a COMPLETED tools/call result carries a resultType marker, and its value is `complete`
edges.evidence: json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:340 — `assert result["resultType"] == "complete"` — over the result of the tools/call driven at json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:331 — `{result, log} = with_log(fn -> call("raw_extras", %{"extras" => %URI{}}) end)`. The test's call helper returns the response's result member, so an error response yields nil and an equality against a string could not hold — which is why the no-error and result-present axes are the SAME observation read at a coarser grain rather than an inference, the reading C1c-ii's two edges on this check already use. The presence axis is the one this edge is really about: it is an IN test on the key, present whatever the value, and an equality assertion against a value cannot hold unless the key is there. THE VALUE AXIS IS SILENT AND THE TWO ANTECEDENTS ARE WHY. The axis requires the resultType of an INPUT-REQUIRED response to be the input_required marker; this unit's response is a COMPLETED tools/call and carries the complete marker, so the axis's antecedent does not hold of it and the axis is not about this case. A reader who reads the axis as unconditional would call it a contradiction, and the difference is stated here so that they can.
edges.note: THE COVERAGE RESULT BEHIND THIS EDGE IS BIGGER THAN THE EDGE. SEP-2322 puts resultType on EVERY result — `dispatch.ex:489-490` says so in terms and puts the complete marker on every one — and the official suite scores the field only inside the input-required family, on the input-required path. This unit and its F-10 sibling are the only members in the declared population that pin resultType on a COMPLETE result, and they do it incidentally, while measuring something else. Recorded once in `the_result_type_marker_the_suite_scores_on_one_path_only`.

member.test: test matching Mcp-Method routes normally; a mismatch is rejected (-32020)
member.register_key: MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest/test matching Mcp-Method routes normally; a mismatch is rejected (-32020)

declared_unmatched.claim_the_slot_names: a request whose `Mcp-Method` header matches its JSON-RPC method routes normally, and one whose header disagrees is rejected -32020
declared_unmatched.why_no_counterpart: `no-oc-server-check` — the suite scores SEP-2243 on the client only. Measured at this tip: 0 of the 119 server rows mention any of the three header families, while the client leg carries 28 rows that do.
declared_unmatched.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is a SERVER rejecting a routing header that disagrees with the body. SRV01's subject is exactly that obligation, and its near miss is the client-side half the suite does carry — which is why a grep for the header names is the wrong instrument here and a leg-scoped sweep is the right one.
declared_unmatched.the_search_that_found_none: a SERVER validating a SEP-2243 routing header against the request body — `Mcp-Method` against the JSON-RPC `method`, and `Mcp-Name` against `params.name` (or `params.uri` on `resources/read`) — and rejecting a mismatch with -32020
declared_unmatched.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: The eleven `http-standard-headers` rows and the seventeen `http-custom-headers` rows — `ClientMcpMethodHeader_tools_call`, `ClientMcpNameHeader_tools_call`, `ClientCustomHeader_Method` and their siblings. A reader who greps `mcp-method`, finds rows and stops would take these for the counterpart. They are all CLIENT-leg, and every one of them scores whether the CLIENT SENDS the header correctly; not one asks what a SERVER does with a header that disagrees with the body it arrived on. The two are different obligations on different peers, and SEP-2243 imposes both.

declared_unmatched.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim has two halves and the search is chosen for the one with no home. The warning half is SRV27's subject — a server diagnosing its own side — and the not-injected half is this one: the suite's content axes would all be SATISFIED by an implementation that injected a block, which is what makes them a near miss rather than a counterpart. They are the closest the suite comes and they are the wrong way round: every one of them asks whether the content array HAS something in it, and the claim here is that the SDK did not PUT something in it. A server that noticed an array-valued structuredContent and quietly injected a serialised-JSON text block to satisfy the MUST would satisfy all five, which is exactly why they cannot be this claim's counterpart. declared_unmatched.why_no_counterpart: `no-oc-scenario` — 0 of all 175 manifest rows on either leg, on a pattern wider than the subject.
declared_unmatched.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is about the INBOUND half of a tools/call — what the handler was handed — and the search is chosen to sweep that vocabulary across every scenario, not only the tools ones. It found the two substitution rows and nothing else, and substitution is the opposite obligation. WHAT THIS ROW DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLAIM: the unit's pipeline at json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:568 takes the head of the content array and decodes its text, so the unit cannot pass unless the result's content is a non-empty array whose first block carries decodable text — which is three of ToolsCallSimpleText's five axes. That is a PRECONDITION of a pipeline and not an assertion, and this file credits an axis to an ASSERTION's subject. Recorded so the choice is visible rather than silent; a reader who counts preconditions as claims should read this row as an edge.
declared_unmatched.the_search_that_found_none: a tool's `arguments` reaching the handler byte-identical — nothing coerced, defaulted, expanded or dropped between the wire and the handler's first line
declared_unmatched.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `PromptsGetWithArgs` — `Get parameterized prompt with argument substitution` — the only row in all 175 matching `(?i)argument`, and a reader who greps for the word lands on it. It is a different obligation on a different endpoint: it scores that a PROMPT template had its placeholders SUBSTITUTED, which is the server transforming the arguments on purpose, where this claim is that a TOOL's arguments are transformed not at all. `ResourcesTemplateRead` is the same shape one endpoint further over. Nearer in spirit is `IgnoreUnexpectedParams`, which is about extra keys being tolerated rather than about the keys that belong arriving unchanged. MEASURED: 0 over all 175 on a pattern deliberately wider than the subject — it would match an `unchanged`, a `verbatim`, a `coerce` or a bare `arguments` row in any scenario. The suite calls tools and scores what comes BACK; no check anywhere asks what the handler was HANDED.

declared_unmatched.why_no_counterpart: `no-oc-scenario` — the suite scores no `extensions` obligation at all. MEASURED over all 175 manifest rows and both legs: zero. The two `-32021` rows a reader might reach for are about an undeclared CLIENT CAPABILITY, which is the other direction.

declared_unmatched.the_search_that_found_none: the `extensions` capability — a server ADVERTISING one under `capabilities.extensions`, a client OFFERING one the server does not support, and the rule that keeps `extensions` and `experimental` apart as two separate capability keys
declared_unmatched.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `DiscoverCapabilitiesMatchHandlers` and `ServerDeclaresPromptsInDiscover` — the two rows that score what `server/discover` advertises, and the rows a reader looking for `does the suite check what we advertise` finds first. They are not counterparts: both range over the NAMED capabilities the schema fixes — `tools`, `prompts`, `resources` — and score them against whether the corresponding handler answers. `extensions` is an OPEN map whose keys the schema does not constrain, so there is no handler for a check to hold an extension against, and neither row reads the key at all. The second near miss is `ServerRejectsUndeclaredCapability` and `MissingCapabilityHttp400`, whose `-32021` a reader may take for the extensions error: their subject is a CLIENT CAPABILITY the client did not declare and the server needed, the opposite direction from a client offering a server an extension it does not support. MEASURED: the strings `extension` and `experimental` do not occur in any of the 175 rows, in any of the six key fields.

member.test: test value encoding — omission and the sentinel's ambiguity rule decode leaves a plain value alone and survives a malformed sentinel
member.register_key: MCP.Protocol.HeaderMirrorTest/test value encoding — omission and the sentinel's ambiguity rule decode leaves a plain value alone and survives a malformed sentinel

declared_unmatched.claim_the_slot_names: `HeaderMirror.decode_value/1` returns a plain header value unchanged, and returns a sentinel-shaped value whose Base64 payload is malformed unchanged rather than raising
declared_unmatched.why_no_counterpart: `no-oc-server-check` — the suite scores SEP-2243 on the client only. Measured at this tip: 0 of the 119 server rows mention any of the three header families, while the client leg carries 28 rows that do.
declared_unmatched.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is the server-side DECODE of a SEP-2243 routing-header value — the step the validation SRV01 searched for is defined in terms of: the spec requires the server to decode the sentinel before comparing, so a unit on that decode is a unit on the first half of that validation. SRV01's pattern and its 119-server-row population are therefore this claim's instrument, and the answer it returned — zero rows on our leg mentioning any of the three header families — covers the decode step as squarely as it covers the comparison.
declared_unmatched.the_search_that_found_none: a SERVER validating a SEP-2243 routing header against the request body — `Mcp-Method` against the JSON-RPC `method`, and `Mcp-Name` against `params.name` (or `params.uri` on `resources/read`) — and rejecting a mismatch with -32020
declared_unmatched.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: The eleven `http-standard-headers` rows and the seventeen `http-custom-headers` rows — `ClientMcpMethodHeader_tools_call`, `ClientMcpNameHeader_tools_call`, `ClientCustomHeader_Method` and their siblings. A reader who greps `mcp-method`, finds rows and stops would take these for the counterpart. They are all CLIENT-leg, and every one of them scores whether the CLIENT SENDS the header correctly; not one asks what a SERVER does with a header that disagrees with the body it arrived on. The two are different obligations on different peers, and SEP-2243 imposes both.

member.test: test decode/1 decodes a request
member.register_key: MCP.ProtocolTest/test decode/1 decodes a request

declared_unmatched.claim_the_slot_names: `Protocol.decode/1` turns an inbound JSON-RPC request into a typed `Request` carrying its id, method and params
declared_unmatched.why_no_counterpart: `no-oc-scenario` — nothing in the suite scores a server's decode of an inbound message. MEASURED over all 175: zero. The one id row scores an echo on the way out.
declared_unmatched.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is about `Protocol.decode/1` turning inbound JSON into a typed request. SRV31's subject is that decode, and the search is leg-wide rather than a grep for `id` because the one row that does mention an id — `HttpServerErrorJsonrpcId` — is about the id on a response the server emits, which is the near miss the entry names.
declared_unmatched.the_search_that_found_none: DECODING an inbound JSON-RPC message into a typed request — that it is recognised as a request at all, and that the `id`'s JSON TYPE survives, a string id staying a string rather than being coerced
declared_unmatched.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `HttpServerErrorJsonrpcId` — `All error responses carry the request JSON-RPC id` — the only row in the 175 that scores an id at all, and the one a reader who greps `id` and stops would take for the counterpart. It is not one, and the direction is what settles it: it reads the id on the RESPONSE the server EMITS and asks whether it equals the one that arrived. That is an echo, and an echo passes whether or not the type survived, because the harness compares the id it sent with the id it got back and both are whatever JSON round-tripped. Nothing anywhere scores the server's DECODE of an inbound message as such — which is unsurprising, since a decode that failed would surface as some other check's failure and never as its own.

declared_unmatched.claim_the_slot_names: `SSE.encode_event/1` emits `event:`, `id:`, `retry:` and `data:` field lines for an event carrying all four, terminated by a blank line
declared_unmatched.why_no_counterpart: `no-oc-scenario` — the suite carries SSE rows and not one of them reads a frame. MEASURED over all 175: zero mention any SSE field line, and the two rows that do open streams count a stream that yields nothing as functional.
declared_unmatched.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is about the BYTES of an SSE frame. SRV30's subject is that syntax, and its near miss is the reason a narrower instrument would mislead: the suite does carry SSE rows, they do run a parser, and they still cannot see framing — so a search that stopped at `is there an SSE check` would answer yes and be wrong about this claim.
declared_unmatched.the_search_that_found_none: the SYNTAX of an SSE frame — the `event:`, `id:`, `data:` and `retry:` field lines, the blank line that terminates a frame, and the folding of a multi-line payload into one `data:` line per line
declared_unmatched.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `ServerSSEStreamsFunctional` — `Multiple POST SSE streams should be functional` — and it is a near miss a reader is very likely to stop at, because the harness genuinely pipes each stream through an SSE PARSER before reading it. It is still not a counterpart, and the decomposition of that check is what settles it: the stream is scored by racing ONE `read()` against a 2 second timer, and a `null` from the timer is not recorded as an error, so a stream whose frames are malformed enough to yield nothing is counted FUNCTIONAL exactly as one that delivers a frame. The event is never decoded and its payload is never compared with the request that opened it. So the check cannot distinguish correct framing from no framing at all, and nothing else in the 175 mentions an SSE field line. The second near miss is `SRV13`'s territory — the SSE response HEADERS — which is a different absence with its own entry and is named here only so the two are not confused.

declared_unmatched.why_this_search_is_this_claims_search: The claim is about a warning emitted at `Plug.init/1` for a risky but legal configuration. SRV32's subject is that diagnostic, and the entry's near miss is why the obvious instrument is the wrong one: `CacheScopeValid` is about the same configuration and PASSES it, so a search that found `a caching check exists` would have answered a question this claim is not asking.
declared_unmatched.the_search_that_found_none: a server DIAGNOSING ITS OWN CONFIGURATION — warning, once and at configuration time rather than per request, about a deployment combination that is legal on the wire but risky in effect
declared_unmatched.the_near_miss_that_is_not_a_counterpart: `CacheScopeValid` — `All cacheScope values are "public" or "private"` — and this is the sharpest near miss in the file, because the two are about the SAME configuration and reach OPPOSITE conclusions about it without contradicting each other. A `cacheScope` of `public` on an identity-dependent response is exactly what this member warns about, and it is exactly what `CacheScopeValid` PASSES: the check's axis is an enumeration over two string literals and has no notion of who the response was built for. So the OC scores the value's VALIDITY and the member scores the deployment's SAFETY, and a server can be green on the first while being the thing the second exists to catch. The general reason for the zero is `SRV27`'s and is not restated: the harness scores messages, and a warning crosses no wire. What is new here is that the diagnostic fires at `Plug.init/1` — once per configuration, never per request — so there is no request for a harness to attach it to even in principle.

A3 §6 state 3 — members adjudicated as having NO OC counterpart among this file's declared 119. They are bucket 1 over this population. The generator asserts each tag guard-checks to state 3 (decodes as `oc:none`, does NOT resolve as an oc key) before counting it. Every one of the 100 names a REGISTERED search by `search_id` — the figure was 47 before C1c-iii-b, 70 after it, and 100 after C1c-iv-a, and it is RE-MEASURED at each slice rather than left behind its own block — which is a step past the client leg: 39 of its 65 rows name one and 26 carry prose the registry limb cannot reach. All 100 here are inside G23b/c/d, and the reason is simply that this file's tickets RAN their searches rather than inheriting them. (This clause read "All 70" at MES-117's delivered tip — the SAME SENTENCE had already been re-measured two clauses earlier, to 100, and the edit stopped at the figure it went looking for. A partial update is the worst shape of stale figure because the field does not look untouched; caught in review, and see `why_the_figure_sweep_missed_four_fields`.)

ONE ROW LEFT THIS BLOCK AT C1c-ii AND FOUR JOINED IT. The leaver is the stateless MRTR round trip, which C1c-i filed here under SRV08 precisely so that the ticket declaring the `input-required-result-*` family would inherit it; that ticket declared it, so the member now carries five edges and SRV08 is deleted with it (G23c refuses an orphan entry). The joiners are the four non-MRTR members of `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTP.ACTest`, whose module C1c-ii had to declare to adjudicate its one MRTR member at all — the same mechanism running the other way, and each of the four records the search, the near miss and the ticket that should pick it up.

the_empty_content_assertions_and_why_eve:
THREE OF THIS MODULE'S MEMBERS ASSERT THAT A tools/call RESULT'S CONTENT ARRAY IS EMPTY, and `ToolsCallSimpleText`'s `content_is_not_empty` axis requires it not to be. ALL THREE ARE SILENT AND NOT `contradicts`, and because `silent` is itself an assertion that can be the false one, the ground is written out here rather than left on three records. THE THREE WERE FOUND BY READING THE PREDICATE OVER THE WHOLE FILE RATHER THAN BY RECALLING WHICH FAMILIES HAVE IT: json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:294 (the C-2 not-injected member), json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:318 (the R-3 camelCase member) and json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:435 (the F-10 keyword-list member). The plan for this slice said `C-2's never-modified and the R-3 three`, which is four and is the wrong four; the measured set is these three.

THE ANTECEDENTS DIFFER, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE IN THE SOURCE. The axis quantifies over the content array of a result returned by a tool that RETURNED CONTENT — the `tools-call-simple-text` scenario calls a fixture tool whose whole job is to produce a text block, and the axis asks whether the array it produced arrived non-empty. Each of the three units drives a handler it has just HANDED an empty content list, so the emptiness is forced by the unit's own construction and is not a behaviour of the SDK at all; what each unit is pinning is that the SDK did not ADD to the list — that an array-valued structuredContent, an unrecognised extras key or a dropped slot 3 leaves the handler's own content untouched. A server that injected a block would fail these units and SATISFY the axis. Two claims satisfied by opposite behaviours are not about the same case.

THE TEST THAT DECIDES IT, AND IT WAS RUN PER MEMBER RATHER THAN ASSUMED: is any of the three empty content arrays NOT construction-forced — a tool that genuinely returned content while the unit still asserts empty? The handler calls are at json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:293, :312 and :426. The first passes an empty content list explicitly; the other two name no content at all and reach the `raw_extras` clause of `MCP.Test.SchemaHandler`, which defaults it to empty. None is a tool that returned content. Had one been, that one would be `contradicts` and would escalate under A3 §3, and it would have been filed that way.

WHERE THE THREE ARE. Two sit on members carrying no edge and are therefore inside bucket-1 rows — the C-2 member under SRV26 and the R-3 camelCase member under SRV27 — and the third is one assertion of a member whose resultType claim is an edge, so it is recorded on that edge's note. A reader who reads the axis as unconditional should read all three as contradictions, and this field is what lets them do it in one place. PM-ratified on MES-119, 2026-09-23.
the_result_type_marker_the_suite_scores_:
THE SUITE SCORES `resultType` ON ONE PATH AND THE SDK PUTS IT ON EVERY RESULT — A COVERAGE ASYMMETRY THIS SLICE FOUND WHILE MEASURING SOMETHING ELSE. SEP-2322 makes `resultType` a member of the Result base rather than of InputRequiredResult: `lib/mcp/server/dispatch.ex:489-490` says so in terms and stamps the complete marker on every result this SDK returns. The official suite's only `resultType` scoring is `ResultTypeIncluded`, in the `input-required-result-result-type` scenario, and all four of its axes are taken over an INPUT-REQUIRED response: the scenario drives a call it expects to be answered input_required and reads the marker off that answer.

SO THE COMPLETE PATH IS SCORED BY NOTHING, and the two members that pin it here are an extras-map warning test (json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:340) and a dropped-slot-3 test (json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:436) — neither about MRTR, both asserting the marker incidentally while measuring a diagnostic. They agree with three of the check's four axes: the no-error and result-present axes, because the test's call helper returns the response's result member and an equality against a string cannot hold over an error or an absent result; and the PRESENCE axis, which is an IN test on the key and is satisfied whatever the value.

THE FOURTH AXIS IS SILENT AND THE JUDGEMENT IS THE SAME ONE THE EMPTY-CONTENT FAMILY RESTS ON. It requires the resultType of an INPUT-REQUIRED response to be the input_required marker; these results are completed calls carrying the complete marker, so the axis's antecedent does not hold of them. It is NOT the case that our SDK would fail that axis on the scenario's own call — C1c-ii's two edges on this same check agree with all four over a real input-required round trip — and if the axis is read as unconditional over every result the suite sees, these two edges are contradictions. The reading is stated so it can be contested; what is not in doubt is the coverage asymmetry underneath it.

the_divergent_despite_agreement_sweep_th.the_claim_this_slice_made_at_its_PLAN_HO:
STATED HERE BECAUSE IT WAS RATIFIED AND BECAUSE A REPORT THAT QUIETLY DROPPED IT WOULD BE THE WORSE ARTEFACT. This ticket's plan reported that the escalation HAD a live instance: that MCP.Transport.SelfCompatibilityTest's three -32020 members — a plain mismatched header, an encoded header naming a different tool, and a sentinel-shaped header that is not valid Base64 — each assert BOTH of `HttpServerHeaderMismatch400`'s required values (HTTP 400, JSON-RPC -32020), agree on both axes, are green while the check is red, and therefore escalate. The arithmetic was right and the ADJUDICATION was wrong, and two independent measurements at execution say so.

(1) THE CHECK'S SUBJECT IS NOT THESE MEMBERS' SUBJECT. Read at the harness build rather than off the description: the check sends `server/discover` with `_meta` naming version `v999.0.0` and an `MCP-Protocol-Version` header naming the negotiated one, so the two values it requires to disagree are the VERSION header and the `_meta` version. A3's own axis says as much — its `http_status` axis `requires` reads `HTTP 400 on a header/_meta version mismatch`. These members vary `Mcp-Name` against `params.name` and send a consistent version header throughout; they never put the check's two values into disagreement and so never reach the behaviour it scores. Under `how_a_silent_axis_was_decided` that is SILENT on both axes, which is the all-silent case, not agreement.

(2) THIS FILE HAD ALREADY ADJUDICATED THE IDENTICAL CLAIM, THE OTHER WAY. C1c-i homed THREE members under SRV01 — including `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest/test Mcp-Name mismatch against params.name is rejected (-32020)`, which is word for word the claim SelfCompatibilityTest's members make through a different fixture — as bucket 1, `no-oc-server-check`, on the measured ground that the suite scores SEP-2243 on the client only. Filing an edge here would have put two contradictory adjudications of one relation in one file. The four members are therefore homed under SRV01 with C1c-i's three.

WHAT THE ERROR WAS, NAMED SO IT IS REUSABLE: the shared -32020 and the shared 400 were read as subject identity. They are the SHAPE of two different obligations — SEP-2575's version-header agreement and SEP-2243's routing-header agreement — and the MCP error code for `a header disagrees with the body` is one code serving both. A grep-shaped reading of the check finds agreement; reading the harness bytes and this file's own precedent finds none.

Three of the seven modules have a nearest check worth naming; four have none on the leg at all and their absence searches are the evidence for that rather than this field.
